Estimate scales of effect jointly across independent data sets

Source: R/joint_scales.R
multiScale_joint.Rd

Experimental. multiScale_joint() combines two or more data sets, each already fitted with multiScale_optim(), and estimates the scale of effect of each landscape covariate jointly. Each data set keeps its own response, model class, and native parameters (for example a Poisson count model and an unmarked occupancy model). What is shared is set by scales and, if you choose, share:

  • scales = "common": one scale for each landscape covariate, used by every data set that contains it.

  • scales = "separate": one scale per data set. This reproduces the separate fits and is the reference for testing whether a common scale is supported.

  • scales = "footprint": one ecological scale, seen through each data set's sampling footprint (see Details). The apparent scale in data set d is sqrt(sigma^2 + footprint[d]^2).

  • scales = "footprint_scaled": as "footprint", with the footprint SDs multiplied by an estimated factor kappa. kappa = 0 is the common scale and kappa = 1 is the stated footprint.

share names landscape covariates whose regression coefficient is also shared across data sets, so the data sets estimate one landscape effect but keep their own intercepts and other coefficients.

Usage

multiScale_joint(
  fits,
  scales = "common",
  footprint = NULL,
  share = NULL,
  cluster = NULL,
  uncertainty = c("hessian", "jackknife"),
  profile = TRUE,
  level = 0.95,
  groups = 20L,
  seed = NULL,
  verbose = TRUE
)

Arguments

fits

Named list of two or more fitted multiScaleR objects from multiScale_optim() with the default backend = "refit", one per data set. The names identify the data sets in the output. Each fit supplies its starting model, its prepared kernel inputs, and starting values. All fits must use the same kernel, Gaussian or exponential. Landscape covariates are matched across data sets by name, so give the same raster layer the same name in every kernel_prep() call.

scales

How the scale of each landscape covariate relates across data sets: one of "common" (default), "separate", "footprint", or "footprint_scaled" for every covariate, or a named character vector with one structure per covariate, such as c(forest = "common", road = "separate"). A covariate that occurs in only one data set always has its own scale.

footprint

Named numeric vector with one sampling footprint SD per data set, in map units, required by the footprint structures. Use 0 for a data set whose response is measured at a point. footprint_sd() converts common sampling geometries to this SD.

share

Optional character vector of landscape covariates whose coefficient is shared across the data sets that contain them. Each such covariate must enter every model as one plain linear term, and the models must use comparable links (all the same link, or a mix of log and complementary log-log, which share the log-intensity scale). Shared coefficients currently require models refitted by update(): glm, MASS::glm.nb, lme4, glmmTMB, and mgcv. Default NULL shares no coefficient.

cluster

Optional site or block identifiers, used to check for and allow dependence between data sets that sample the same places. Either the name of a column present in every model's data, or a named list with one vector per data set aligned with that model's data rows (or unmarked sites). Default NULL.

uncertainty

"hessian" (default) takes standard errors from the Hessian of the joint log-likelihood, which assumes the data sets are independent. "jackknife" deletes one group of clusters at a time and refits, which allows dependence within clusters, including between data sets that share a site. Its Wald limits use a t distribution with one fewer degree of freedom than the number of replicates. It requires cluster and is not yet available for unmarked models.

profile

Logical. If TRUE (default), compute profile-likelihood intervals for every estimated parameter.

level

Confidence level for the intervals. Default 0.95.

groups

Number of jackknife groups when uncertainty = "jackknife". Clusters are assigned to groups at random. Default 20, or the number of clusters if smaller.

seed

Optional integer seed for the jackknife group assignment.

verbose

Logical. If TRUE (default), report progress.

Value

An object of class multiScaleR_joint, a list with

  • parameters: estimated parameters (scales in map units, kappa, shared coefficients) with standard errors and Wald and profile-likelihood limits.

  • scales: the apparent scale of each covariate in each data set.

  • fits: named list of component multiScaleR fits.

  • comparison: log-likelihoods, parameter counts, and the likelihood-ratio test against separate scales.

  • residual_correlation: correlation of residuals between data sets at shared clusters, when cluster is supplied.

  • logLik, df, nobs, vcov (parameters on the optimizer scale: log scales, kappa, coefficients), structure, footprint, share, standardization, uncertainty, optim, and call.

Details

The joint likelihood. For a given set of scales, each data set's model is refitted exactly as multiScale_optim() refits it, and its maximized log-likelihood is returned. multiScale_joint() maximizes the sum of these log-likelihoods over the scale parameters (and shared coefficients). With scales = "separate" and no shared coefficient the sum separates, and the result equals the separate fits. Because the joint fit treats the data sets as independent pieces of evidence, it is valid when they are independent given the covariates. Data sets that sample the same sites may share unexplained site effects; supply cluster to measure the residual correlation at shared sites, and use uncertainty = "jackknife" when it is not negligible.

Comparing structures. The returned object reports the likelihood-ratio test of the fitted structure against separate scales. With two or three data sets this test has little power, so a nonsignificant result is weak evidence for a common scale. Fit several structures and compare them with stats::AIC() (the fits have stats::logLik() methods) or stats::anova(). To test kappa = 0, compare a "common" fit with a "footprint_scaled" fit in stats::anova(). That value lies on the boundary of the parameter space, so anova() refers the statistic to a mixture of chi-square distributions, which halves the p-value for one kappa. With a single data set that has a footprint, kappa can match that data set's apparent scale exactly, so the ecological scale then rests on the point data sets alone.

Sampling footprints. A response is often measured over an area, not at a point: counts within a fixed radius, detections by an acoustic recorder, a camera viewshed, or animals detected by distance sampling. If the ecological response follows the landscape smoothed with a Gaussian kernel of scale sigma, then a response averaged over a footprint with per-axis SD tau follows the landscape smoothed by the convolution of the two, whose per-axis variance is sigma^2 + tau^2. Data sets with larger footprints therefore show larger apparent scales even when the ecological scale is the same. The relation is exact for a Gaussian footprint and for a covariate that enters the linear predictor linearly; for a disk or square footprint it matches the second moment, and on a log or logit link it is a first-order approximation that holds while the landscape effect varies little within one footprint. Footprint structures require the Gaussian kernel.

Shared coefficients. For each shared covariate, every data set's model is refitted with that term replaced by a fixed offset equal to the shared coefficient times the covariate. The covariate is standardized with one center and spread pooled across the data sets, evaluated at the ecological scale, so the coefficient has the same meaning in every data set.

Component fits. $fits holds one multiScaleR object per data set at the jointly estimated scales, with standard errors from the joint fit. Use them with plot.multiScaleR(), plot_marginal_effects(), kernel_scale.raster(), and predict() as for any other fit. Two cautions apply: summary(fit, profile = TRUE) and profile_sigma() on a component profile that data set alone, and a shared coefficient enters a component's model as an offset named .msr_joint_offset, so effect curves and maps of that covariate are not yet available from the component.

See also

multiScale_optim(), footprint_sd(), profile_sigma(). vignette("v16-joint-data-sets", package = "multiScaleR") works through an example with three surveys, shared sites, and a sampling footprint.

Examples

# \donttest{
# Two independent surveys of one landscape: Poisson counts and binary
# detections. Both respond to `bin1` and `cont2` at the same true scales.
rs <- sim_rast(user_seed = 123, dim = 100, resolution = 30)
rs <- terra::subset(rs, c("bin1", "cont2"))

counts <- sim_dat(alpha = 0.5, beta = c(0.75, -0.75), kernel = "gaussian",
                  sigma = c(75, 150), type = "count", n_points = 60,
                  raster_stack = rs, max_D = 450, user_seed = 1)
occ <- sim_dat(alpha = 0, beta = c(1, -1), kernel = "gaussian",
               sigma = c(75, 150), type = "occ", n_points = 80,
               raster_stack = rs, max_D = 450, user_seed = 2)

in_counts <- kernel_prep(counts$pts, rs, max_D = 450, verbose = FALSE)
in_occ <- kernel_prep(occ$pts, rs, max_D = 450, verbose = FALSE)

fit_counts <- multiScale_optim(
  glm(y ~ bin1 + cont2, family = poisson,
      data = data.frame(y = counts$obs, in_counts$kernel_dat)),
  in_counts, verbose = FALSE)
fit_occ <- multiScale_optim(
  glm(y ~ bin1 + cont2, family = binomial,
      data = data.frame(y = occ$obs, in_occ$kernel_dat)),
  in_occ, verbose = FALSE)

joint <- multiScale_joint(list(counts = fit_counts, occ = fit_occ),
                          scales = "common", verbose = FALSE)
joint
#> 
#> Joint scale-of-effect fit (experimental)
#> Data sets: counts (glm, n = 60); occ (glm, n = 80)
#> Kernel: gaussian
#> 
#> Scale structure
#>  covariate structure   data_sets shared_coefficient
#>       bin1    common counts, occ              FALSE
#>      cont2    common counts, occ              FALSE
#> 
#> Joint parameters (scales in map units)
#>    parameter estimate    SE 95% lower (profile) 95% upper (profile)
#>   sigma:bin1    63.66 12.79               42.97               96.93
#>  sigma:cont2   175.50 51.50               92.27              429.20
#> 
#> Apparent scale in each data set
#>  data_set covariate  sigma    SE 95% lower (profile) 95% upper (profile)
#>    counts      bin1  63.66 12.79               42.97               96.93
#>    counts     cont2 175.50 51.50               92.27              429.20
#>       occ      bin1  63.66 12.79               42.97               96.93
#>       occ     cont2 175.50 51.50               92.27              429.20
#> 
#> logLik = -137.046 (df = 8), AIC = 290.091, n = 140
#> Against separate scales: LR chi-square = 2.322, df = 2, p = 0.313
#> 
#> Note: Standard errors assume the data sets are independent given the covariates.

# Compare with one scale per data set
separate <- multiScale_joint(list(counts = fit_counts, occ = fit_occ),
                             scales = "separate", profile = FALSE,
                             verbose = FALSE)
AIC(joint, separate)
#>          df      AIC
#> joint     8 290.0912
#> separate 10 291.7697
# }
